html:
The Oxus civilisation, also called the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex (BMAC), was a Bronze Age culture of fortified oasis towns in southern Central Asia, in what is now Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Afghanistan and northeastern Iran. It flourished from roughly 2250 to 1700 BCE, though dates are still debated.

It was identified only in the 1970s, when the archaeologist Viktor Sarianidi dug sites in the Murghab delta, the old region of Margiana. The best known is Gonur Depe, a walled compound with palaces, temples and large cemeteries. Similar sites lie along the Oxus river in Bactria.

The people farmed with irrigation canals, worked bronze, silver and gold, and carved fine stone seals. They traded far:

  • with the Indus civilisation to the southeast
  • with Elam and Mesopotamia to the west
  • in lapis lazuli from the mountains of Badakhshan

The towns declined after about 1700 BCE, as the Indus cities did. Herders of the Andronovo culture from the northern steppe moved into the area in the same years. Many scholars think the meeting of steppe people and oasis farmers here shaped the Indo-Iranian peoples, and that some of them later took part in the Indo-Aryan migrations into South Asia. This is likely but not settled.
